workload.description: Browse-heavy storefront: 95% catalogue reads, 5% cart/checkout writes

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: m6i.large — AWS EC2 us-east-1 / On-Demand / Linux / shared tenancy / 730 h per month; instance-hour only (excludes EBS, data transfer); x86-64 (Intel Ice Lake). Band: zero-width: within the pinned scope the hourly list rate is a single exact published number with no variance. Month length (672-744 h), burstable credit surcharges, Savings Plans and Spot are OUT-OF-BAND modifiers, named per row, not band edges.

citations.note: $0.096/h x 730 = 7008c/month. Cross-checked to the cent against the AWS Price List Bulk API (version 20260904231117).

components.name: Redis: catalogue, price and session cache

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: cache.r6g.large — AWS ElastiCache us-east-1 / On-Demand / Redis engine / standard support / 730 h per month; node-hour only. Band: zero-width at the Redis/Memcached standard-support rate. The Valkey engine is CHEAPER and Extended Support is DEARER; both are different products/support states, not a price range for this row, so they are named here rather than used as band edges.

db.m6i.large — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.178/h Single-AZ x 730 = 12994c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class.

components.name: Read replica — catalogue and search reads

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: db.m6i.large — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.178/h Single-AZ x 730 = 12994c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class. A read replica is billed as its own full instance, at the same rate as a primary.

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: kafka.m5.large — AWS MSK us-east-1 / On-Demand / provisioned broker / 730 h per month; broker-hour only (excludes storage and data transfer). Band: zero-width: single published broker-hour rate in the pinned scope.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 8,000 req/s peak (a mid-size retailer's flash-sale hour); 95% of requests are catalogue/search reads and 5% are cart or checkout writes

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: 85% catalogue cache hit-rate: 15% of browse requests and 40% of searches fall through to the read replica (search is the colder path)

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: The Redis node is sized for WORKING-SET MEMORY, not request rate, so its utilisation reads low (~8%). That is the correct shape for a catalogue cache, not spare headroom you can bank on — losing the node moves 7,600 req/s onto the replica

assumptions.subject: app
assumptions.statement: ~1,000 req/s per application instance: template rendering plus 2-3 backend calls per request. Ten instances is the sizing decision that keeps the tier at 80% at peak

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Single PostgreSQL primary at ~8,000 write-path req/s; reads are served by one replica. Replication lag is NOT modelled by the v1 analytical engine — a stale-price or oversold-inventory read is a real risk this design does not quantify

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Order events go to a 3-broker Kafka cluster (~20,000 msg/s per broker) which runs at ~1% utilisation at 400 orders/s. THREE m5.large BROKERS IS A DURABILITY AND QUORUM CHOICE, NOT A CAPACITY ONE: the order log is money, so it does not run on burstable instances. It is ~30% of the compute bill for ~1% of the load, and that is deliberate. Payment authorisation itself is out of scope here (see the payments reference design)

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The load balancer is priced at 0: an ALB's hourly + LCU charge is per load balancer, not per instance, and the engine multiplies cost by instance count. Add ~$16/month plus LCU to any total you quote

_library.summary: Browse-heavy online store with a catalogue cache, a read replica and an order event stream.
